hints: Recall the point at which gravitational potential is defined to be zero.
Consider whether the gravitational force between masses is attractive or repulsive, and whether work is done by the field as a mass approaches from infinity.
walkthrough: State that gravitational potential at infinity is defined to be zero.

Explain that because the gravitational force is attractive, work is done by the field (or energy is released / work got out) as an object moves from infinity to a point in the field, making the potential less than zero (i.e. negative).

ai_rubric.observable: States that (gravitational) potential at infinity is defined as zero or is zero.
Explains that because the (gravitational) force is attractive, work is done by the field / work is got out / work is done as object moves from infinity, so the potential is negative.

hints: Read the gravitational potential $\phi$ at $x = 0.1 \times 10^{12}\,\mathrm{m}$ and $x = 1.2 \times 10^{12}\,\mathrm{m}$ from Fig. 1.2.
Calculate $\Delta E_{\mathrm{k}} = m|\Delta\phi|$ and determine whether the rock moves to a deeper potential well (higher speed) or not.
walkthrough: From Fig. 1.2, read the potentials: $\phi_1 = -10.0 \times 10^8\,\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$ at $x = 0.1 \times 10^{12}\,\mathrm{m}$ and $\phi_2 = -14.0 \times 10^8\,\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$ at $x = 1.2 \times 10^{12}\,\mathrm{m}$.
Calculate the change in kinetic energy: $\Delta E = m \Delta\phi = 180 \times (14 - 10) \times 10^8 = 7.2 \times 10^{10}\,\mathrm{J}$.
Since the potential becomes more negative (potential energy decreases), kinetic energy increases, so the change is an increase.

ai_rubric.observable: Calculates change in energy using $\Delta E = m\Delta\phi = 180 \times (14 - 10) \times 10^8$ with potential values read from Fig. 1.2.
States that the change in kinetic energy is an increase.

hints: Find the peak (maximum) potential $\phi_{\mathrm{max}}$ between $x = 0.1 \times 10^{12}\,\mathrm{m}$ and $x = 1.2 \times 10^{12}\,\mathrm{m}$ on Fig. 1.2.
Set the initial kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ equal to the minimum energy required to reach this peak potential.
walkthrough: From Fig. 1.2, identify the maximum potential barrier between $x = 0.1 \times 10^{12}\,\mathrm{m}$ and $x = 1.2 \times 10^{12}\,\mathrm{m}$, which is $\phi_{\mathrm{max}} = -4.4 \times 10^8\,\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$.

Calculate the energy required to reach this peak from $x = 0.1 \times 10^{12}\,\mathrm{m}$ (where $\phi = -10.0 \times 10^8\,\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$): $\Delta E = 180 \times (10 - 4.4) \times 10^8\,\mathrm{J}$ (or energy per unit mass $= (10 - 4.4) \times 10^8\,\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$).

Equate initial kinetic energy to this required energy: $\frac{1}{2} \times 180 \times v^2 = 180 \times (10 - 4.4) \times 10^8$, giving $v = \sqrt{2 \times 5.6 \times 10^8} = 3.3 \times 10^4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
